title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service used by approximately 25 million people to record virtual meetings on platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams is accused of recording conversations without obtaining consent from all participants and sharing them with the company to train its AI systems. The service can automatically join meetings if an account holder has integrated their calendar, creating a condition where recording occurs without affirmative consent from everyone in the conversation. This represents a deployment failure where the system's integration with calendar software enabled recording outside the scope of what meeting participants expected or agreed to.

The lawsuit claims the company violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws by using recordings to train AI systems. While the company's privacy policy includes a checkbox for AI training purposes, the plaintiff alleges many users remain deceived about this practice. The company states it anonymizes data before using it for speech recognition improvement, but whether this deidentification is effective is not established. A federal court in California has allowed the privacy claims to proceed, meaning the allegations have not yet been adjudicated as fact.

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit claims that Otter's transcription service, which is used by approximately 25 million people to record virtual meetings on platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams, records conversations and shares them with the company to train its AI systems without properly notifying all meeting participants. Plaintiff Justin Brewer alleges his privacy was invaded when he discovered Otter secretly recorded a confidential conversation. The lawsuit contends that Otter violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and records meetings to derive financial gain.

The suit raises concerns about Otter's practices, particularly when the software automatically joins meetings if an account holder has integrated their calendar and records without getting consent from all participants. While Otter's privacy policy states it receives explicit permission through a checkbox for AI training purposes, the lawsuit maintains that many users are still deceived about this practice. The company has faced recent scrutiny after users shared stories on social media about recordings capturing sensitive business information and concerns about data sharing with third parties. Otter claims it anonymizes data before using it to improve its speech recognition systems, but the lawsuit questions the effectiveness of this deidentification process.
